newsitem.title: UK: UK manufacturing exporters see bright future - poll.
newsitem.headline: UK manufacturing exporters see bright future - poll.

text.p: British exporters are relatively optimistic about their business prospects in both the short and long term, according to the DHL third quarter Export Indicator survey published on Friday.
The poll of over 500 managers responsible for exports in British manufacturing showed almost three-quarters anticipated an increase in new export orders over the next year.
Thirty-eight percent of exporters viewed order expectations as very good or excellent over the next three months, with that figure rising to 59 percent over the next year.
This optimism has pushed the Export Confidence Index up to 41, six points higher than the previous quarter, DHL said.
"It is encouraging to note the rising optimism shown by exporters throughout the country," said Glyn Jones, Commercial Director at DHL International (UK).
"This is also supported by views on employment prospects, indicating the return of the feelgood factor is here to stay."
Just under half of exporters surveyed believed employment would rise over the next 12 months.
The DHL poll said EU markets continued to offer British manufacturing exporters the greatest potential for growth, with 51 percent anticipating an increase in exports there over the next 12 months.
China, Latin America, India and EFTA countries also showed improved prospects.
The poll said that since the beginning of the year, understanding of the implications of a single European currency among British exporters had diminished.
Just 44 percent of respondents said they were familiar with its consequences, with 54 percent unfamiliar, from 53 percent and 44 percent respectively in Q1 1996.

Exporters were also less optimistic about the impact of a single currency on business. Just 54 percent believed it would help, three percent down on the first quarter of 1996, and 32 percent expected it to hinder.
"Those against a single currency cite the idea that it is an impossible dream as the prime reason," the poll said.
"According to our survey, confusion is growing (about the single European currency), indicating the need for widespread education rather than political point scoring," said Jones.
